title: Lower courts and tenure: the cases
ask: Give the two cases on abolishing lower courts or judgeships, and what each held.
items: Ocampo v. Secretary of Justice (1955): 7 of 11 found RA 1186 void, short of two-thirds; the prevailing four: the power to abolish courts includes reducing or recategorizing judges; abolition is not removal
De La Llana v. Alba (1982): BP 129 valid; abolition in good faith is not removal (“no tenure to a non-existent office”); a renaming is not abolition; consult the Court on incumbents

title: When a court reorganization is valid
ask: What must a law abolishing or restructuring lower courts satisfy?
items: A court below the Supreme Court (Congress cannot touch the Court’s Sec. 5 jurisdiction)
A real abolition, not a renaming (Brillo v. Enage)
Good faith: no judges singled out, no “evil purpose”
The Court consulted on separated incumbents (De La Llana)
Since 1987: it must not undermine the security of tenure of judges (Sec. 2)
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 2; De La Llana v. Alba
hook: Real, in good faith, and ask the Court.

title: RA 11459 (2019), the Judges-at-Large Act
ask: State the key features of RA 11459.
items: 100 Regional Trial Judges-at-Large and 50 Municipal Trial Judges-at-Large
No permanent salas; assigned by the Supreme Court as acting or assisting judges as public interest requires
The Court fixes the length of each assignment
The JBC recommends appointees, and later the permanent sala for each
RTC: natural-born, 35, 10 years of practice; first level: natural-born, 30, 5 years

title: The JBC’s seven members
ask: Name the seven members of the JBC, ex officio first.
items: The Chief Justice (ex officio Chairman)
The Secretary of Justice (ex officio)
A representative of Congress (ex officio; one seat, one vote)
A representative of the Integrated Bar
A professor of law
A retired Member of the Supreme Court
A representative of the private sector
hook: Three ex officio, four regular; Congress gets one.

title: Congress’s seat in the JBC: the cases
ask: Give the two cases on Congress’s representation in the JBC and their holdings.
items: Chavez v. JBC (2012; 2013 Resolution, 9–3): “a representative” means one seat, one full vote; seven members, not eight; casus omissus; past acts valid (operative fact)
Umali v. JBC (2017, 9–5): Chavez stands as stare decisis; any Senator or Representative may represent all of Congress; six-month rotation valid; more seats need an amendment

title: Filling a Chief Justice vacancy
ask: What did Dulay and Adaza settle about a Chief Justice vacancy?
items: The Chief Justice is one of the “Members of the Supreme Court” the President appoints from a JBC list (Dulay; Adaza)
The JBC may act without its ex officio Chairman; the senior Justice who is not an applicant presides (Dulay)
The 90 days from the vacancy are mandatory and “imperative” (Sec. 4(1); Adaza)
Pending cases cannot hold up the appointment (Adaza)
The election ban does not apply to the Judiciary; the JBC should list before the vacancy (De Castro v. JBC)

title: The Court and the JBC: what remedy?
ask: Which remedies lie against the JBC, and why?
items: Supervision: oversight of the JBC’s compliance with its own rules, not control of its choices (Jardeleza)
Certiorari: yes, for grave abuse, under the expanded judicial power (Jardeleza; Villanueva; Umali)
Mandamus: no, nominating is discretionary (Jardeleza; Villanueva)
Declaratory relief: not with the Supreme Court; no right to be listed (Villanueva)

title: Nominating: the cases
ask: Give the three cases on how the JBC nominates, with their holdings.
items: Jardeleza v. Sereno (2014): integrity means moral character, not legal strategy; an objected applicant gets notice and time to answer; deemed included
Villanueva v. JBC (2015, 11–0): the five-year rule for first-level judges is a reasonable criterion, but must be published
Aguinaldo v. Aquino III (2016): nomination is a qualification; no clustering for simultaneous vacancies; seniority follows the commissions

title: The 2020 Revised JBC Rules: numbers to remember
ask: State the key numbers in the 2020 Revised Rules of the JBC (as amended in 2021).
items: Judges seeking promotion: 5 years in their present rank (Rule 3, Sec. 3)
Appellate courts, Ombudsman, Deputies, Special Prosecutor, LEB: at least 4 votes to be nominated (Rule 8, Sec. 3)
At most 7 nominees per vacancy; more rounds until at least 3 (Rule 8, Sec. 4)
Supreme Court: 2.5 years left to serve for appellate justices, constitutional commission chairs, the SolGen and Cabinet secretaries; 5 years for others (Rule 8, Sec. 1)
The age rule does not apply to sitting Justices applying for Chief Justice
src: JBC No. 2020-01, as amended by Resolution No. 03-2021

title: The Judiciary’s three budget guarantees
ask: What three guarantees does Art. VIII, Sec. 3 give the Judiciary?
items: Fiscal autonomy: full flexibility to allocate and use its resources (Bengzon v. Drilon)
No reduction below the previous year’s appropriation
Automatic and regular release once approved
hook: All three released automatically; only the Judiciary has a floor.

title: What makes the commissions independent
ask: List the constitutional safeguards of the commissions’ independence.
items: Declared “independent” (Art. IX-A, Sec. 1)
Fixed, staggered seven-year terms without reappointment; no temporary or acting appointments
Appointment by the President with CA consent
No other office or profession, and no conflicting interests, during tenure (Sec. 2)
Salary not decreased during tenure (Sec. 3)
Appoint their own officials and employees (Sec. 4)
Fiscal autonomy and automatic release (Sec. 5)
Their own procedural rules (Sec. 6)

title: Who sits in each commission
ask: How many members does each commission have, and what professions are required?
items: CSC: a Chairman and 2 Commissioners; proven capacity for public administration
COMELEC: a Chairman and 6 Commissioners; college degree; a majority, the Chairman included, lawyers with 10 years’ practice
COA: a Chairman and 2 Commissioners; CPAs with 10 years’ auditing or lawyers with 10 years’ practice; never all of one profession
All: natural-born, at least 35, not candidates in the election just before
hook: Three, seven, three; seven-year terms; a majority of all.

title: How a commission decides and is reviewed
ask: State the rules on how the commissions decide and how their rulings reach the Court.
items: A majority of all the Members: 4 for the COMELEC, 2 for the CSC and COA (Art. IX-A, Sec. 7)
Decide within 60 days from submission
COMELEC election cases: division first; reconsideration by the en banc (Art. IX-C, Sec. 3)
No 4 votes to grant reconsideration, even after rehearing: denied; the division stands (Legaspi)
COMELEC and COA: certiorari to the Supreme Court within 30 days (Rule 64); CSC: petition for review to the Court of Appeals (Rule 43)
src: Art. IX-A, Sec. 7; Art. IX-C, Sec. 3

title: The civil service: the cases
ask: Give the five civil service cases and their holdings.
items: De los Santos v. Mallare (1950): tenure covers the unclassified service; only confidential, policy-determining, highly technical posts are at pleasure
Cuevas v. Bacal (2000): CES tenure attaches to rank, not position
Buklod ng Kawaning EIIB v. Zamora (2001): good-faith reorganization is not removal
TIDCORP v. CSC (2013): CSC rules cannot override a charter exemption
Flores v. Drilon (1993): an elective official cannot be appointed to another office during tenure

title: Positions terminable at pleasure
ask: Which positions are excluded from security of tenure, and what marks each?
items: Primarily confidential: close intimacy, trust against betrayal of personal confidence or State secrets
Policy-determining: makes policy rather than executes it
Highly technical: skill or training in a superior degree
src: Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(2); De los Santos v. Mallare

title: Signs of a bad-faith reorganization (RA 6656, Sec. 2)
ask: What signs show that a reorganization is in bad faith?
items: A significant increase in positions in the new staffing pattern
An office abolished and another performing substantially the same functions created
Incumbents replaced by less qualified people
An office reclassified to perform substantially the same functions
The order of separation violated
src: RA 6656, Sec. 2; Buklod ng Kawaning EIIB

title: The COMELEC: the cases
ask: Give the three COMELEC cases and their holdings.
items: Legaspi v. COMELEC (2016, 8–7): four votes to reverse a division; otherwise the motion is denied and the division stands
Sula v. COMELEC (2023, 12–0): residual power to set plebiscite dates; it frames the question; fraud must be proved specifically
Goh v. Bayron (2014, 12–0): a line item for recall exists; augment from savings; hold the recall
src: Art. IX-C, Secs. 2(1) and 3; Art. IX-A, Secs. 5 and 7

title: The COA: the cases
ask: Give the three COA cases and their holdings.
items: DBP v. COA (2002, 15–0): the power to audit is not exclusive; scope, rules and disallowance are; COA findings prevail
Special Audit Team v. CA (2013, 13–0): the COA may create special audit teams; exhaust COA remedies first
Funa v. MECO (2014, 15–0): MECO is not a GOCC, but its government-sourced fees are auditable

title: The three attributes of a GOCC
ask: What three attributes make an entity a GOCC?
items: Organized as a stock or non-stock corporation
Performing a public function
Owned or controlled by the government (for a non-stock corporation: a majority of members who are government officials, or a substantial government role in choosing the board)
src: Funa v. MECO; Administrative Code, Sec. 2(13)
